question: As recorded, none. The ledger labels P-30's AUC ~0.85 as T1 and sets it against P-66's MCI vs CN accuracy (72.7%), but P-30 reports no MCI vs CN result. Judged on the printed figures (condition 6), both papers report the same comparison: AD vs MCI discrimination in ADNI Alzheimer's-spectrum subjects from structural T1 MRI. The task, population class and channel match. The pair qualifies on this re-filed comparison, not on the recorded claim_b.
metric: ROC-AUC with ROC-AUC (P-30 0.85 vs P-66 0.595); accuracy with accuracy agrees in direction (P-30 validation 0.78 vs P-66 0.58).

figures.P-30: AD vs MCI (2+1)D CNN, whole-brain T1: AUC 0.85 +/- 0.046 (per model 0.86, 0.94, 0.86, 0.80, 0.83), from five CV models scored on a 15% subject-level test set held out at the start. Validation accuracy 0.78 +/- 0.032. No 95% interval is reported. The test set is 15% of 427 subjects, about 64 (about 33 AD and 31 MCI). Hanley-McNeil with A = 0.85: Q1 = 0.85/1.15 = 0.7391; Q2 = 2(0.7225)/1.85 = 0.7811; SE = sqrt([0.1275 + 32(0.7391 - 0.7225) + 30(0.7811 - 0.7225)]/(33*31)) = 0.0486; interval [0.755, 0.945]. At the scan level (76/76) it is [0.788, 0.912]; a t-interval on the fold mean gives [0.793, 0.907]. Accuracy 0.78 with n of about 363 (the 85% CV remainder): Wilson [0.735, 0.820].
figures.P-66: AD vs MCI hippocampus/amygdala CNN + radiomics + age/sex fusion: AUC 0.595, ACC 58% (radiomics alone 0.575/57%, CNN alone 0.577/56.6%). Five repetitions of a random 80/20 image split over 602 AD and 948 MCI images from 199 and 200 subjects. No interval is reported. Smallest defensible n: 20% of 399 subjects, about 80 (40/40). Hanley-McNeil with A = 0.595: Q1 = 0.595/1.405 = 0.4235; Q2 = 2(0.3540)/1.595 = 0.4439; SE = sqrt([0.2410 + 39(0.4235 - 0.3540) + 39(0.4439 - 0.3540)]/1600) = 0.0635; interval [0.471, 0.720]. With image counts (about 120/190) it is [0.530, 0.661]. ACC 0.58 with n = 80: Wilson [0.471, 0.682].

matched_figure_check: No matched figure exists. For AD vs MCI, P-66 reports only hippocampus/amygdala ROI variants (radiomics alone AUC 0.575, CNN alone 0.577, fusion 0.595); P-30 reports only whole-brain variants (2D CNN 0.84, 3D CNN 0.81, (2+1)D 0.85). Neither paper reports the other's input representation, validation split or subject selection, so nothing in the papers reconciles the gap.
performance_validity: Neither paper meets the Section 3.5 exclusion. P-30's AUC is 0.85 (highest single model 0.94, below 0.97); P-66's is 0.595.

candidate_explanations.difference: Input representation: the whole-brain T1 volume downsampled to 32x32x32 (P-30), against cropped hippocampus and amygdala ROIs with 4x1746 PyRadiomics features plus age and sex (P-66).
candidate_explanations.quote: The dataset then resized into 32 × 32 × 32 dimensions.

candidate_explanations.difference: Input representation (P-66 side): ROI crops only.
candidate_explanations.quote: The input images of the left and right hippocampus have been resized to 16x40x24 after eliminating the black background areas around them.

candidate_explanations.difference: Label definition and subject selection. P-30 keeps AD patients who stayed AD and MCI patients without multiple reversions or conversions, which could make the classes more separable. P-66 randomly selects baseline ADNI subjects without a stability filter.
candidate_explanations.quote: AD patients were diagnosed as AD and stayed stable during the follow-up. MCI patients were diagnosed as MCI, EMCI or LMCI and did not encounter multiple reversions and conversions and did not convert back to AD.

candidate_explanations.difference: Scan selection. P-30 uses about 2.3 to 2.5 scans per subject, not restricted to baseline (507 scans of 223 AD, 507 of 204 MCI), so AD scans may include later, more advanced visits. P-66 uses baseline images.
candidate_explanations.quote: Although ADNI database incorporates much higher number of scans for MCI subjects, 507 scans of 223 AD patients and 507 scans of 204 MCI patients were selected, to avoid any possible imbalance in computational experiments.

candidate_explanations.difference: Validation design. P-30 uses a 15% subject-level test set scored by five CV models; P-66 uses a random 80/20 split of images, not subjects, repeated five times. An image-level split would, if anything, inflate P-66, the opposite of the observed direction.
candidate_explanations.quote: randomly dividing the MRI data for each classification dataset into a sizeable training and validation set (80 % of images) and a testing set (20 % of images).

candidate_explanations.difference: P-66's own account of its low AD vs MCI figure, milder AD cases in ADNI. P-30 also samples ADNI, so this explains the gap only if the AD samples differ in severity (see scan selection).
candidate_explanations.quote: However, this was not the case, primarily due to the less severe nature of the AD cases in the ADNI dataset.

reason: The ledger's recorded pairing (P-30's AD-vs-MCI AUC against P-66's MCI-vs-CN accuracy) is a misread and is not itself a discrepancy. On the figures both papers print for the same question, the pair meets every condition: AD vs MCI discrimination from structural MRI in ADNI, with AUC 0.85 (P-30) against 0.595 (P-66). The derived 95% intervals do not overlap ([0.755, 0.945] vs [0.471, 0.720]), no matched figure reconciles them, and neither result is near ceiling. The candidate explanations (input representation, subject and scan selection, split design) are not shown by either paper to be sufficient. The ledger record would need re-filing on AD vs MCI AUC.

quotes.quote: 507 scans of 223 AD patients and 507 scans of 204 MCI patients were obtained for the computational experiments.
15% of the data was split as test set at the very beginning. The test set was reserved until the end of the train/validation process and it was used for calculating the auc scores only.
and in 0.85 + /-0.046 average auc score, (auc score per fold: [0.86,0.94,0.86,0.80.,0.83]).
Considering the minimal preprocessing and subject level data split, the proposed model performed comparably well to the recent studies for similar classiﬁcation problems

In the term of AD vs MCI, radiomic-based algorithm alone obtained ACC of 57 % and AUC of 57.5, CNN-based algorithm obtained ACC of 56.6 % and AUC of 57.7 and their fusion showed ACC of 58 % and AUC of 59.5.

We utilized three datasets, including AD (199 cases, 602 images), MCI (200 cases, 948 images), and CN (200 cases, 853 images), to perform binary classification (AD vs. CN, AD vs. MCI, and MCI vs. CN).
The performance evaluation method employed in this study was the 5-fold cross-validation method.
